title: Dirty Hands: The Art and Crimes of David Choe
description: Harry Kim's feature documentary follows David Choe from Congo travel and Los Angeles graffiti through juvenile detention, commercial illustration, imprisonment in Japan, artistic success, and the dissatisfaction that survives it.
summary: Harry Kim's feature documentary follows David Choe from Congo travel and Los Angeles graffiti through juvenile detention, commercial illustration, imprisonment in Japan, artistic success, and the dissatisfaction that survives it. The film's structure is associative rather than strictly chronological: studio interviews, family testimony, artwork, music and handheld travel footage repeatedly return to the question of why Choe makes things and destroys stability. Early passages distinguish his attraction to drawing on walls from gang territory, then connect shoplifting, graffiti and gambling to distrust of adult authority. The documentary does not romanticize the consequences. Juvenile lock-up, a riot and looting, a large police response, a public foot chase and jail deprivation are narrated alongside Choe's own admissions, jokes and later efforts to explain the pattern. A key middle movement shows art becoming paid work: approaching adult magazines, an overheard complaint turning into an ice-cream-shop mural, inviting other painters onto walls, and making a twelve-women calendar that attracts hostile replies. Imprisonment in Japan becomes a hinge. Friends find the work harder to read afterward; Choe says his career accelerated so quickly after release that he never stopped to process the sentence. The final third covers deliberate destruction inside carefully rendered work, resistance to being made legible, the Facebook-office commission, repeated cycles of finding and losing God, and the realization that sales and freedom do not produce lasting relief. The closing whale-name anecdote and party montage refuse a tidy recovery story. The route uses an owner-supplied 480p film copy and contains 36 explicit human-reviewed scene notes. Those notes are documentary navigation, not transcript speech. Claims about crimes, motives and mental state remain attributed to the film and its participants; the archive does not add diagnosis or convert illegal acts into instructions.

connections.note: The director appears within a long relationship of filming, travel and collaboration; the documentary's intimacy is part of its evidence and part of its point of view.
Brazzaville and rural travel footage frame the film and interrupt the biographical chronology with danger, curiosity and performance.
Choe separates drawing from gang territory while explicitly connecting illegal acts to distrust of adults; the film preserves both his distinction and the real consequences.
The sentence is treated as an artistic and psychological hinge, but participant observations about its effects are not clinical diagnosis.
The office commission appears as daily-use commercial art and a success marker; the film predates the later mythology around the equity's value.
A Jesus image built from Old Testament words connects family faith, image-making and Choe's repeated claim that he finds and loses God.
The late admission that shows, sales and freedom remain fleeting complicates any simple crime-to-redemption arc.

publication_restrictions.rule: Preserve Choe's causal account as self-explanation, not a general excuse for crime or a factual diagnosis.
Do not extract the riot and looting material as instruction or celebration.
Keep arrest and sentence claims attributed to the documentary record.
Do not diagnose trauma or other conditions from the reported post-Japan change in artwork.
Do not back-project later Facebook-stock valuations into this film's contemporary account.
